title: An Bhulseochaid Aigein / Simple Past Tense
bridge: In Irish, the simple past tense is formed differently from English. Unlike English, Irish verbs don't always add '-ed' or change spelling for the past tense. Instead, Irish uses a system of initial mutations and specific endings. Be cautious with irregular verbs, as they can be quite different from their English counterparts. For example, 'to go' in Irish is 'dul', but its past tense is 'chuaigh', which doesn't resemble the English 'went'.
rule: For regular verbs in Irish, the simple past tense is formed by adding specific endings to the verbal stem, often accompanied by initial mutations. The endings depend on the verb class and the subject. Irregular verbs have unique past tense forms that must be memorized. Common patterns include: 1) Verbs ending in -igh often drop the -igh and add -eadh (e.g., 'scríobh' → 'scríobhadh'). 2) Verbs ending in -eoir often add -igh (e.g., 'caint' → 'cainteadh'). 3) Irregular verbs like 'bí' (to be) and 'téigh' (to go) have completely different forms (e.g., 'bhí' and 'chuaigh').

title: An Présaint Cheanaigh / Present Progressive
bridge: In Irish, the present progressive (or 'present continuous') is formed using the verb 'bheith' (to be) + the verbal noun, similar to English's 'to be + -ing'. However, unlike English, Irish doesn't use this form for temporary actions or to emphasize ongoing actions. Instead, it's often used to describe actions happening now or around now, and can also express future intentions. Be careful not to overuse it as you would in English.
rule: The present progressive in Irish is constructed with the present tense of 'bheith' (to be) followed by the verbal noun. The verbal noun is formed by adding '-áil', '-í', '-adh', or other suffixes to the verb stem, depending on the verb. For example, 'togháil' (choosing) from 'tóg' (take/choose). The present tense of 'bheith' is: táim (I am), tá tú (you are), tá sé/sí (he/she is), táimid (we are), tá sibh (you pl. are), tá siad (they are).

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate the '-ing' form without using 'ag' (at) before the verbal noun. Remember, in Irish, the structure is always 'tá + subject + ag + verbal noun'.

'Déanamh' is the verbal noun of 'déan' (do).
'Feiceáil' is the verbal noun of 'feic' (see).
Use 'ag labhairt' for ongoing actions like talking.
Simple present progressive for plural subjects.

title: Tá áireamh agam / I'm going to
bridge: In Irish, the future with 'going to' is often expressed using the phrase 'tá áireamh agam' or 'tá mé ag dul chun'. Unlike English, Irish does not use a direct equivalent of 'going to' but instead relies on the present tense of 'tá' (is) followed by the verbal noun or 'ag dul chun' (going to). Be cautious not to directly translate 'going to' as it can lead to incorrect structures in Irish.
rule: To express the future with 'going to' in Irish, use 'tá áireamh agam' or 'tá mé ag dul chun' followed by the verbal noun. For example, 'Tá áireamh agam ____' or 'Tá mé ag dul chun ____'. The verbal noun is the base form of the verb without the 'to'. This structure is used for near future intentions or plans. Note that Irish does not have a direct equivalent of the English 'going to' and relies on context and these specific phrases.

title: An Todhchaí Shimplí / The Simple Future
bridge: In Irish, the simple future is often expressed using the word 'beidh', which is the future form of the verb 'bí' (to be). This is different from English, where 'will' is commonly used. Be careful not to directly translate 'will' into Irish, as it doesn't have a direct equivalent. Instead, focus on using 'beidh' followed by the verbal noun, which is a key difference from English.
rule: The simple future in Irish is formed by using 'beidh' (the future of 'bí') followed by the verbal noun. For example, 'beidh mé ag nóiseoireacht' (I will be singing). The verbal noun is the same for all persons and numbers. Note that some verbs have irregular verbal nouns, so it's important to learn these. Unlike English, Irish does not use a subject-verb agreement in the future tense, making it simpler in some ways but requiring attention to the correct verbal noun.

title: Comparádh agus Superlatives / Comparatives and Superlatives
bridge: In Irish, comparatives and superlatives often involve more morphological changes than in English. While English typically adds '-er' or '-est' or uses 'more' and 'most', Irish changes the initial consonant of the adjective (eclipsis or lenition) and adds specific particles like 'níos' for comparatives and 'is' for superlatives. Be cautious with irregular forms and the placement of these particles, as they differ from English structures.
rule: To form comparatives in Irish, use 'níos' before the lenited adjective (e.g., 'níos fearr' = 'better'). For superlatives, use 'is' before the eclipsed adjective (e.g., 'is fearr' = 'best'). Irregular adjectives change completely (e.g., 'maith' → 'fearr'). Note that 'níos' and 'is' come before the adjective, unlike 'more' and 'most' in English. Superlatives also require the definite article 'an' before the noun.

title: Verba Modhacha / Modal Verbs
bridge: In Irish, modal verbs like 'caithfidh' (must), 'ba cheart' (should), and 'ní mór' (have to) are used similarly to English modals, but they often require different sentence structures. Unlike English, Irish modals frequently appear at the beginning of the sentence and may trigger lenition (séimhiú) on the following verb. Be cautious of word order and initial mutations, which are less common in English.
rule: Irish modal verbs express necessity, obligation, or advice. Key modals include 'caithfidh' (must), 'ba cheart' (should), and 'ní mór' (have to). These verbs typically precede the main verb, which is often in the verbal noun form (e.g., 'ag + verb'). Lenition (séimhiú) is applied to the verbal noun if possible. For example, 'Caithfidh mé an teach a dhéanamh' (I must build the house). Note that Irish modals do not change form based on the subject, unlike English modals.

title: Verba Aiseata / Reflexive Verbs
bridge: In Irish, reflexive verbs are used similarly to English, but with a key difference: the reflexive pronoun always matches the subject in person and number. Unlike English, where 'myself' can be used for 'I' or 'me', Irish uses specific pronouns like 'mé féin' for 'I myself'. Be careful not to directly translate English reflexive pronouns, as Irish often requires a different structure.
rule: Reflexive verbs in Irish are formed by adding the reflexive pronoun to the verb. The reflexive pronouns are: 'mé féin' (myself), 'tú féin' (yourself), 'sé/sí féin' (himself/herself), 'muidne féin' (ourselves), 'sibhse féin' (yourselves), 'siad féin' (themselves). The verb often remains unchanged, but some verbs require the preposition 'le' before the reflexive pronoun. Reflexive verbs are used to indicate that the subject and object of the verb are the same.

title: Pronómna Obachta / Object Pronouns
bridge: In Irish, object pronouns are used similarly to English, but their placement and form can differ. Unlike English, Irish object pronouns often come before the verb in questions and after the verb in statements. Additionally, Irish has a T-V distinction with 'tú' (informal you) and 'sé/sí/siad' (he/she/they) having distinct object pronoun forms, which doesn’t exist in English. Be cautious of the pronoun 'é' (him/it), which can be confused with the English 'he' but is used more broadly.
rule: Object pronouns in Irish replace direct and indirect objects. They are placed immediately after the verb in statements and before the verb in questions. The pronouns are: 'mé' (me), 'tú' (you), 'é' (him/it), 'í' (her/it), 'sé' (him), 'sí' (her), 'sinn' (us), 'sibh' (you pl.), 'iad' (them). Note that 'é' and 'í' can refer to both masculine/feminine nouns, unlike English. In questions, the pronoun precedes the verb, e.g., 'An bhfuil é agat?' (Do you have it?).

common_error.explanation: English speakers often incorrectly use subject pronouns ('me') instead of object pronouns or fail to use the correct Irish structure. Remember, Irish object pronouns replace the object and are placed according to sentence type (after verb in statements, before in questions).

title: Adverbtaí Coitianta / Common Adverbs
bridge: In Irish, frequency adverbs like 'always', 'often', and 'never' generally come after the subject and before the verb, unlike in English where they typically appear before the verb. Be careful not to place them at the end of the sentence as this is incorrect in Irish. Additionally, Irish frequency adverbs do not change form, regardless of the subject or tense.
rule: Frequency adverbs in Irish are placed immediately after the subject and before the verb. Common adverbs include 'go minic' (often), 'go leor' (frequently), 'go deo' (always), 'riamh' (ever), and 'ná habair' (never). These adverbs remain the same in all tenses and with all subjects. For example, 'Tá mé ag dul go minic' (I often go) and 'Ní théann sé go deo' (He never goes).

title: Prepositions of Time / Preipéisí Ama
bridge: In Irish, prepositions of time often differ from English, especially with specific time expressions. For instance, 'at' in English is often translated as 'ag' in Irish, but 'ar' is used for days. Be cautious with 'in' and 'on', as Irish uses 'i' for months and years, and 'ar' for dates. Unlike English, Irish prepositions often require the lenition (séimhiú) of the following word, which can be a common trap for learners.
rule: Irish prepositions of time follow specific patterns: 'ag' is used for times of day (e.g., 'ag a haon' - at one), 'ar' for days of the week (e.g., 'ar an Luan' - on Monday), and 'i' for months and years (e.g., 'i Márta' - in March). Lenition is applied after 'ag' and 'i' when followed by a consonant (e.g., 'ag an' becomes 'ag an'). Exceptions include 'ar maidin' (in the morning) and 'ar feadh' (for a period of time).

title: Conjunctions / Conjuncideanna
bridge: In Irish, conjunctions like 'agus' (and), 'ach' (but), and 'nó' (or) function similarly to their English counterparts, but their placement can differ. For instance, 'ach' often comes after the verb in a sentence, unlike 'but' in English. Additionally, Irish uses 'mar' for 'because' and 'nuair' for 'when', which have distinct structures compared to English. Be cautious of word order and the use of 'má' for 'if', which can be more formal than the English equivalent.
rule: Conjunctions in Irish are used to connect words, phrases, or clauses. Key conjunctions include: 'agus' (and), 'ach' (but), 'nó' (or), 'mar' (because), 'nuair' (when), and 'má' (if). 'Agus' and 'nó' are straightforward, but 'ach' often follows the verb in a sentence. 'Mar' introduces a reason, while 'nuair' is used for time-related conditions. 'Má' is used for conditional statements and is more formal than 'if' in English. Note that word order in Irish can be more flexible, but conjunctions typically follow the main verb in the clause.

title: An Phhraseach Coimeádach / The Present Perfect
bridge: In Irish, the present perfect (Perfecto compuesto) is formed using the present tense of the verb 'to be' (bí) followed by the past participle of the main verb, similar to English. However, unlike English, Irish does not use auxiliary verbs like 'have' for this tense. Additionally, the past participle in Irish often requires the use of the word 'ar' before it, which can be confusing for English speakers. Be cautious of word order and preposition usage, as these differ from English.
rule: The present perfect in Irish is constructed as follows: Tá + ar + past participle. The verb 'tá' (is) conjugates based on the subject. The past participle is formed by adding 'ar' before the verb, but some verbs have irregular forms. This tense is used to describe actions completed in the past with a result in the present, similar to English. Note that the word order is more flexible in Irish, but the basic structure remains consistent.

common_error.wrong: Tá mé a léamh an leabhar.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often try to directly translate the English structure 'have + past participle' into Irish. However, Irish uses 'tá' with 'ar' and the past participle, and the word order is different. Avoid using 'a' (to) before the verb, as it is incorrect in this context.

examples.note: Focus on the basic structure: 'tá' + 'ar' + past participle.

title: Imperativí / Imperatives
bridge: In Irish, imperatives are often more direct than in English, especially in the tu (singular you) form. Unlike English, Irish does not use the subject pronoun in the affirmative imperative, and the negative form requires the particle 'ná' before the verb. Be cautious with verb endings, as they can differ from the present tense, especially in the negative.
rule: In Irish, the affirmative imperative for 'tú' (you singular) is formed by using the verbal stem without a subject pronoun. For 'sibh' (you plural), add '-aig' or '-íg' to the stem. The negative imperative uses 'ná' before the verb, with the verb often taking the same form as the present tense. For example, 'Tabhair' (Give!) becomes 'Ná tabair' (Don't give!).

common_error.explanation: English speakers often mistakenly use 'ní' (which negates statements) instead of 'ná' for imperatives. 'Ná' is specifically used for negative commands in Irish.

title: Sustantivos Contables e Incontables / Count and Uncount Nouns
bridge: In Irish, countable nouns (like 'leabhar' - book) change when pluralized, often by adding 'a' or 'í', while uncountable nouns (like 'airgead' - money) remain the same. Unlike English, Irish doesn't use 'some' or 'any' with uncountable nouns; instead, it uses the noun alone or with 'a' for quantity. Be cautious: some nouns are countable in English but uncountable in Irish, like 'hair' (English) vs. 'gruaig' (Irish, uncountable).
rule: Countable nouns in Irish have a singular and plural form, often marked by suffixes like 'a' or 'í'. Uncountable nouns refer to mass or abstract concepts and do not change in form. To express quantity with uncountable nouns, use 'a' (of) + noun, e.g., 'a lán airgead' (a lot of money). Articles like 'an' (the) are used with both types, but uncountable nouns never take a plural form.

He has a lot of money.

title: Rudaí áirithe / Some and Any
bridge: In Irish, 'some' and 'any' are translated as 'rudaí áirithe' and 'ar bith', respectively. Unlike English, Irish uses 'ar bith' more frequently in questions and negatives, while 'rudaí áirithe' is used in affirmative statements. Be cautious not to directly translate 'some' and 'any' without considering the context, as Irish often omits these words in certain sentences.
rule: In Irish, 'rudaí áirithe' is used to refer to a specific, unspecified quantity in affirmative statements. 'Ar bith' is used in questions and negatives to indicate an unspecified quantity. Compounds like 'cúigear ar bith' (any five) and 'beagán' (a little) are also common. Note that Irish often omits quantifiers in casual speech, relying on context instead.

title: Go leor / Much, many, a lot of
bridge: In English, 'much' and 'many' are used for uncountable and countable nouns respectively, while 'a lot of' is more informal and works for both. In Irish, 'go leor' is the equivalent for all cases, but it behaves differently grammatically. Unlike English, 'go leor' always comes after the noun and requires the genitive case for nouns, which can be a trap for English speakers.
rule: 'Go leor' is used to express 'much', 'many', or 'a lot of' in Irish. It always follows the noun and the noun must be in the genitive case. For example, 'arán' (bread) becomes 'aráin' in the genitive. There are no exceptions based on countability, unlike in English. The structure is: Noun (genitive) + go leor.

title: Na hOrchoimeachtaí Comhráideacha / Relative Clauses
bridge: In Irish, relative clauses often use the pronoun 'a' (which) instead of 'that' as in English. Unlike English, Irish relative pronouns agree in gender and number with the noun they refer to. Be careful with word order: Irish places the verb before the subject in relative clauses, which is the opposite of English.
rule: Relative clauses in Irish are introduced by relative pronouns such as 'a' (which), 'ar' (that), or 'den' (of the). The relative pronoun agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. The verb in the relative clause typically precedes the subject. For example: 'An fear a bhfuil an leabhar aige' (The man who has the book). Exceptions include when the relative pronoun is omitted, which is common in spoken Irish.
